message.content:
Based on my search, here's what you need to know about vitamin B12 intake:

## No Established Upper Limit

Vitamin B12 **does not have a Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL)** because it has very low potential for toxicity. The Food and Nutrition Board at the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine did not establish a UL for vitamin B12, as it is generally considered safe even at high doses.

## Why B12 Is Considered Safe

- **Water-soluble**: B12 is a water-soluble vitamin, meaning any excess is excreted through urine rather than stored in the body
- The Institute of Medicine states that **"no adverse effects have been associated with excess vitamin B12 intake from food and supplements in healthy individuals"**

## Recommended Daily Amounts

| Group | RDA |
|-------|-----|
| Adults (14+ years) | 2.4 mcg |
| Pregnancy | 2.6 mcg |
| Breastfeeding | 2.8 mcg |

## What Counts as "Too Much" in Practice

While there's no official toxic threshold, some considerations exist:

- **Supplements of 25 mcg/day or higher** may be associated with increased risk of bone fractures in some studies
- **Oral doses up to 1,000 mcg/day** are commonly used to treat deficiency and are generally considered safe
- High-dose supplements (500–1,000 mcg) are often recommended for those with absorption issues since only a small percentage is actually absorbed

## Possible Side Effects at High Doses

Though rare, some people taking very high amounts may experience:
- Skin reactions (acne, rosacea-like rashes, flushing)
- Mild gastrointestinal upset (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea)
- Headaches, dizziness, or tingling in hands and feet

## Important Caveats

- **Folic acid interaction**: High folic acid intake (>1 mg/day) can mask B12 deficiency symptoms, potentially leading to nervous system damage if untreated
- **Kidney disease**: Very high B12 doses may cause complications in people with kidney disease
- **Pernicious anemia**: People with this condition cannot absorb B12 properly and need injections rather than oral supplements

## Bottom Line

There is essentially **no "too much" B12** in terms of toxicity for healthy individuals. However, you should still:
- Consult a healthcare provider before taking high-dose supplements
- Not use high-dose B12 to self-treat without proper diagnosis
- Be aware that more isn't necessarily better—your body can only absorb so much at once

1. https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminB12-HealthProfessional/
2. https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/vitamin-b12/
3. https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/nutritional-disorders/vitamin-deficiency-dependency-and-toxicity/overview-of-vitamins
4. https://www.health.com/how-much-vitamin-b12-per-day-should-you-take-11896280
5. https://www.health.harvard.edu/healthy-aging-and-longevity/should-you-take-a-vitamin-b12-supplement
6. https://www.mayoclinic.org/drugs-supplements-vitamin-b12/art-20363663
7. https://biologyinsights.com/can-you-overdose-on-vitamin-b12/
8. https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/vitamin-b/
